item.title: Iran ramps up attacks on Gulf countries after U.S. strikes
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: Bahrain and Kuwait said Wednesday that they intercepted weapons launched by Iran after the U.S. carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran appears to be stepping up attacks on America's Persian Gulf allies as tension ratchets back up across the region.A U.S. official called the Tuesday strikes on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island a defensive response to Iranian forces "targeting U.S. personnel and assets" in the region. The strikes came hours after Iran said it targeted a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain for the third time in less than a week. Those attacks were all intercepted, U.S. authorities said.A crew member was missing Wednesday after a ship belonging to the United Arab Emirates' state oil company ADNOC was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, the energy firm said. Eleven people were injured, and search and rescue operations were ongoing, according to ADNOC.

item.title: 5 EU nations make plans to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda
item.description:
London — Five European Union countries have announced a plan to establish a deportation center in Rwanda next year to which they hope to send migrants whose asylum requests they have rejected.
The plan has echoes of President Trump's controversial initiative to deport migrants to third countries to which they have no links, and an effort by a previous British government that failed to clear legal hurdles. It is an attempt by the five European nations to address widespread concerns about mass-migration that have fueled political change across the continent, but it is far from guaranteed to succeed, or even to get off the ground.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have reached an agreement in principle with Rwanda to open a so-called "return hub" in the landlocked African nation in 2027. Unlike the U.S. program, the plan would only apply to migrants who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain in Europe and subsequently been placed under a deportation order.
Rather than being returned to their countries of origin, some migrants would instead be transferred to Rwanda, where they would have the option of staying or returning to their home countries. The plan is intended to provide the European nations an alternative for cases in which deportation to a migrant's country of origin is not possible, either because those countries will not accept them, or due to circumstances that could endanger the migrant if they return.
Many European governments have sought to reduce the number of migrants entering their countries, or already present without permission, in the face of mounting political pressure from voters.
As an example of the kind of statistics fueling that public concern, there were some 230,000 foreign nationals in Germany at the end of 2025 who were legally required to leave the country, according to the Die Welt newspaper, yet government figures show fewer than 23,000 deportations were carried out during the year.

item.title: Inside China's race to get humanoid robot helpers into our homes
item.description:
Wuhan, China — In the large lobby of a three story building in Wuhan, China, a child-size yellow robot greets visitors with a dance. It sways along to traditional Chinese music while robots twice the size stand on either side of the stage, beating loud drums to the rhythm. The little robot then moves on to another dance, bopping along to a pop tune that makes people smile and laugh.
The small humanoid robot's agility makes it look almost lifelike. Then it stops, and the crowd is ushered on to see the real wonders inside the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center.
On the top floor, more than 100 computer science and engineering graduates toil at individual work stations wearing gloves and outfits equipped with motion and tactile sensors, while cameras record their every movement.
One pours water into a jug; another places cutlery and chopsticks into a container. The graduate at the next table unscrews a flashlight and removes the battery, then replaces it.
All the movements are done slowly, meticulously and repeated over and over again, with the actions recorded as valuable data from the cameras and sensors that can be used to train the company's humanoid robots.
An engineering graduate works on training a humanoid robot at the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center in Wuhan, China.
CBS News
"It was fun at first," said 22-year-old intern Mei. "It gets a little boring in the middle. But it's such a proud moment when we get the model trained."
Mei is one of nearly 1 million engineering graduates China's universities are estimated to be churning out every year. The U.S., by comparison, sends about 140,000 young engineers into the job market annually.

item.title: China's Xi greets Trump at airport ahead of planned summit with Putin
item.description:
President Trump arrived in China on Wednesday after starting a multiday Asia swing in the Philippines. He's scheduled to meet in Shenzhen, a hub of China's tech industry, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit on Thursday.
Mr. Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying such a meeting "may not be possible" but the president is "prepared" for one.
Xi greeted Mr. Trump on a red carpet as he walked off Air Force One in Shenzhen.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Mr. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting Wednesday ahead of the planned trilateral summit. Peskov also said Putin had already held a meeting with Xi, during which they discussed the war in Ukraine. Mr. Trump and Putin may also discuss Ukraine, Peskov said.
President Trump salutes as he stands with China's President Xi Jinping after arriving on Nov. 28, 2026, at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport.
Mandel NGAN/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
Putin mentioned his recent discussions in Moscow with Mr. Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during his meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Peskov said.
"The three leaders have a lot to discuss, given the unstable situation in the world," Putin's senior aide Yury Ushakov told reporters in Shenzhen, according to Russian state broadcaster Vesti. He did not confirm the plan for an initial bilateral meeting between Putin and Mr. Trump on Wednesday, but said they might meet during a formal dinner.
It "will not be a single event," Ushakov said of the possibility of Trump-Putin encounters on Wednesday. "It will take place both standing, on the steps, and while seated."

item.title: 2,000-year-old bog woman was beheaded in possible ritual killing
item.description:
London — An investigation into the death of a young Iron Age woman whose remains were preserved in a Northern Ireland bog for more than 2,000 years has found that she was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," when she was between 15 and 22 years old.
The enquiry into the remains known as the "Ballymacombs More Woman," discovered in a peat bog in central Northern Ireland in October 2023, determined that she was decapitated from behind, most likely with a bladed weapon.
"While the precise circumstances surrounding her death remain unknown, the evidence suggested that she may form part of a wider tradition of ritualized killing and sacrifice," said the Ulster Museum, which hosted a coroner's investigation into the two-millennia-old killing. It said the woman's death appeared similar to others documented among Iron Age bodies discovered in bogs across northwest Europe.
The More Woman's body dates from between 343 to 1 B.C., from the prehistoric Iron Age period.
A photo provided by Northern Ireland's police service shows the remains of the "Ballymacombs More Woman," which lay preserved in a peat bog for more than 2,000 years before being discovered in 2023.
Police Service Northern Ireland
"Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare," Hannah Crowdy, head of curatorial for Northern Ireland's National Museums, told CBS News partner network BBC News. "She's the first of her kind in Northern Ireland."
"This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious," Crowdy added. "There's been a really intensive period of research … To honor her, it's important to tell her story and bring that to the fore."

item.title: Voyager 1 sets distance record of 1 "light day" from Earth
item.description:
NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.
An artist's impression of NASA's Voyager spacecraft.
NASA
Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets "Grand Tour" before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.
Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.
As of 5:16 a.m. EST Wednesday, Voyager 1, sailing through space at nearly 38,000 mph, was expected to pass the one-light-day milestone, so far away that radio signals, traveling at 186,000 miles every second, need 24 hours to reach flight controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
That means the 13-member team will have to wait until Thursday for Voyager 1's first post-light-day signal to confirm the achievement.
Voyager 1 was launched atop a Titan rocket on Aug. 2, 1977. NASA will mark the spacecraft's 50th anniversary next year.
NASA
